articles.title: With Lonnie Bunch’s ouster, Trump chills free speech at the Smithsonian
articles.summary: What obviously led to Bunch’s abrupt resignation was Trump on his case.
articles.body:
The Smithsonian Institution is a group of museums, education and research centers, created by Congress as a trust in 1846 “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge.” About 62 percent of its funding comes from the federal government. The Smithsonian is supposed to be independent of the executive branch. A bipartisan board of regents runs the show.

The Smithsonian’s first Black chieftain, Lonnie G. Bunch III 73, announced his retirement last week after more than seven years in the institution’s top job. Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, lauded Bunch for “excellence in the telling of our nation’s story,” stating that the Smithsonian had “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.”

The truth is Trump forced Bunch out of his job, heralding a tectonic shift in institutional purpose.

Over nearly 40 years in various roles at the Smithsonian, Bunch proved himself as an effective advocate and diplomat, and an incredible fundraiser. As the institution’s guiding spirit, he was also a forceful voice on race, particularly after the 2017 Charlottesville incident and George Floyd’s 2020 Minneapolis murder.

Bunch is a man of considerable soft-spoken warmth. I met him in New York last June when he was honored by the conservative Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History for his contributions to history, education and scholarship. He left an indelible impression. The son of two teachers, his love of history was palpable as he said eloquently, “there is nothing more powerful than a people, than a nation, steeped in its history. And there’s nothing more noble than honoring all our ancestors by remembering.”

What obviously led to Bunch’s abrupt resignation was Trump on his case. Out of some perverse desire for political cleansing of artistic expression, Trump waged a chilling campaign on the Smithsonian to purge what he called “improper ideology,” going so far as to threaten the institution’s federal funding and challenge its autonomy.

Bunch told the New York Times it was not the Trump freeze-out that spurred his departure, but admitted that at times, his role had been “stressful”.

“When you’re Black in America, you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right?” he said. “You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table.”

Trump’s drive to gut the Smithsonian began in March 2025 with an executive order that accused the institution of spouting a “divisive” and “race centered” message. The White House subsequently identified exhibits it found objectionable, principally targeting discussions of race, slavery, immigration and transgender identity.

The sparks flew further in May 2025 when Trump said he had fired Kim Sajet, longtime director of the National Portrait Gallery, calling her highly partisan and a supporter of diversity, equity and inclusion. The Smithsonian’s regents pushed back. After a tense meeting, they publicly affirmed that personnel decisions belonged to Bunch, with oversight by the board. Sajet resigned four days later , saying her departure was the best way to serve the institution.

Pressure soon expanded beyond personnel. Trump went ballistic posting on social media in August 2025 that the institution “is OUT OF CONTROL,” and only discusses “how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been.”

“We have the “HOTTEST” Country in the World, and we want people to talk about it, including in our Museums,” he added.

This spring, Bunch said he was proud of what the Smithsonian had achieved under his leadership despite the barrage of Trump attacks. “Nothing can take that away,” he said . “So, I’m trying to make sure I don’t let this moment steal my joy. ”

The White House next produced a July 4 report about the National Museum of American History that accused its director of “ radical activist ideology ” and charges the museum with undermining “faith in American institutions.” The board called for its 21 museums to review their content for partisanship or bias. But the administration began its own review of exhibitions, wall text and social media to assess “tone, historical framing and alignment with American ideals.”

After the report, the salvos continued. Museum director Anthea M. Hartig came under fire at two congressional hearings . Trump ordered posting of warning signs to convey his view that the museum did not accurately reflect American history. The signs never appeared.

Later, the White House escalated again, with a 162-page report accusing the National Museum of American History of portraying the American story as one of “regret, tragedy, and shame.”

Bunch, who generally avoided publicly confronting Trump, forcefully pushed back. He told Smithsonian employees the report was “not a fair characterization” of the museum and said its work remained driven by “scholarship, accuracy, and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America’s story.”

“America is not afraid of its own history,” Bunch said. “My job is always to help the Smithsonian tell complicated stories that really allow us to understand the fullness of the American experience.” The institution’s 180-year-old history is “a reservoir…for understanding of science, of history, of art.”

“For me, it is really building on the Smithsonian’s long history of saying, ‘No matter what, we will be independent.’”

Bunch plans to depart by the end of the year.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: The Movement: Friction among conservative media grows as Trump’s approval falls
articles.summary: President Trump came to power in 2016 and again in 2024 on a wave of conservative media backing, as right-wing podcast, radio and TV hosts built brands off supporting him and his movement. As the president’s approval wanes with voters, many of those same voices have become more willing to call balls and strikes —…
articles.body:
President Trump came to power in 2016 and again in 2024 on a wave of conservative media backing, as right-wing podcast, radio and TV hosts built brands off supporting him and his movement.

As the president’s approval wanes with voters, many of those same voices have become more willing to call balls and strikes — and others in the conservative media ecosystem are becoming quicker to push back at the critics.

Online, that friction has sparked up in recent months over issues as different as childcare subsidies for stay-at-home parents and the price of a steak burrito.

The diverging camps within the media coalition that once rallied behind Trump highlight the divisions emerging across the conservative movement on a number of hot-button issues — just as the race for Trump’s successor gets going.

Erick Erickson , a conservative radio host and commentator who had been a Trump critic but then endorsed him in 2020 and 2024, told The Hill that he’s noticed he gets more backlash when he speaks against the Trump administration’s moves than he used to.

“As the president is headed more into lame-duck status, and we are on the verge of the midterms. There is more, I would say, I would call it bullying, almost to try to get people to shut up or toe the line,” Erickson said. “It’s a much more intense, organized effort, and ironically, it is by the groups in D.C. that used to be the people on the outside who would cajole what was at the time the establishment … they’ve kind of become the establishment.”

Erickson mentioned those in Washington close to Vice President Vance , as well the Heritage Foundation and the Conservative Partnership Institute , closely linked conservative heavy hitters in D.C., as part of the crackdown.

“Anyone in Washington who is kind of hitching their wagon now to the Vance campaign are the most aggressive at pushing back on any sort of criticism,” he said.

Douglas Blair , spokesperson for Heritage Action for America , said the group encourages “rigorous, substantive debate among conservatives about the future of our country.”

“We won’t always agree on policy, but we know solutions can only come from the right because the left has become so out of step with average Americans. We will iron out our disagreements, and the best answers will inevitably emerge,” he said.

The rise in right-wing voices willing to speak their minds is not necessarily without precedent for this point in an election cycle. Erickson said that while some commentators have started speaking out more, others, like Ben Shapiro and Dana Loesch , have been doing so this whole time and are now getting more buzz.

“There is this moment in every administration in the last two years, where voices that were once quiet speak up until the next leader is chosen, and they get quiet again and try to be on the team,” Erickson said. “But I mean, you’ve seen pretty consistently a Dana Loesch, a Ben Shapiro, people like that willing to stand up and just, I mean, speak their mind on issues they haven’t, they’ve never really been silent, but they’re starting to get more traction now from other people.”

The recent debate over a plan to make stay-at-home parents eligible for a childcare subsidy exposed those tensions. Loesch, among many others in different factions of the right, was vocally against the program , which she compared to welfare and blasted for being “big-government.”

Loesch also appeared critical of Trump’s idea to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans keep their majority in Congress, which the president floated at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas last week.

“Dear heavens man, what,” Loesch wrote in response to a video of Trump making this suggestion.

For Loesch, a conservative columnist and radio show host based in Missouri, this debate is between the “grassroots” and the “establishment” about who owns the GOP, and it stretches back to Tea Party days.

“A reminder — the GOP had the debate with voters on big government back in 2010. Grassroots mopped the floor with them,” Loesch wrote in a recent social media post. “Are voters more inclined towards government expansionism now? Post-conservative Republicans are by way of defending the same big government ideas that led to massive GOP losses in 2008. Time will tell if voters are, but that’s what post-conservative (don’t say liberal, it insults Tocqueville!) establishment acolytes believe, with enough propaganda.”

Even if the philosophical debate has been going on a while, the new turn is that conservative audiences — Erickson’s and Loesch’s listeners — are starting to warm to the criticism of the status quo. That reflects what polling shows, too: Trump’s approval rating is under 40 percent, and the congressional majority is looking shaky for the incumbent GOP majority.

Erickson said his listeners used to chime in accusing him of criticizing Trump “just to say you’re criticizing Trump.” But now, especially on certain issues that have economic effects on voters’ lives, like the Iran war and the tariffs, he said they’re starting to hear him.

“The one where I think I have turned people in my direction is the tariffs,” Erickson said. “In 2025 I was criticizing them, and most of my audience was very aggravated with me for criticizing the tariffs. And at this point, they’ve all recognized that the tariffs are not a good idea.”

As the midterms close in, and the race for 2028 starts up, whoever looks to succeed Trump will have to swim against that tide. The obvious front-runner is Vance, but Erickson said he’s hoping to see more options since many conservatives aren’t Vance’s biggest fans.

“To the extent that any conservatives are willing to speak out and and think differently than the administration or what the Vance wing of the party wants, you’re getting blowback there to try to silence people and not have an open primary in 2028,” Erickson said. “I think there are a lot of people who want to make it a coronation, and a lot of the pressures within the conservative movement right now are designed to stifle any criticism in that direction.”

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

GOP DIVERGES ON ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PANIC

As warnings of an artificial intelligence “apocalypse” swirl online and in headlines in recent days, Republican leaders in Congress find themselves at odds with many of their members, and at risk of giving Democrats an opening to take decisive steps toward guardrail policy.

A wave of AI researchers and engineers — and now founders — at top tech companies are saying it’s time to slow the pace of AI development and set up guardrails to prevent the technology from getting out of hand. But as a political question, GOP leaders are struggling to buck President Trump and the wing of their party who still want aggressive AI competition with China.

Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) are dismissing the idea that guardrails for AI are necessary. Meanwhile, Republicans in both chambers see an opportunity for legislation. And Democrats are preparing to seize the moment, urging Johnson to keep the House in session for the next two weeks to move forward on legislation that would stem the tide.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said Monday that any legislation to regulate AI should have “a light touch,” saying Congress and tech companies could take some action while not setting the U.S. back behind competitors, like China.

But Trump and Republican leaders are facing a tide of public opinion that is generally anxious about unregulated AI development, especially among young people. That could be politically risky on the eve of the midterms, as the same leaders have, for the most part, also tied the Republican majority to Trump’s name and agenda. Johnson and his leadership team all spoke at the Republican National Committee midterm convention in Dallas last week, where they praised Trump’s achievements.

SORORITY SISTERS WANT COURT TO RECONSIDER DEFINITION OF ‘WOMAN’

A group of sorority sisters from the University of Wyoming chapter of Kappa Kappa Gamma is trying again to get a court to consider their years-long challenge to their sorority, which changed its eligibility criteria to allow “women and individuals identifying as women” to join. The sisters are claiming that that change fundamentally affected the makeup of the organization, and that the 2022 vote to admit a transgender student was conducted in bad faith.

The 10th Circuit, based in Denver, heard oral arguments Monday as the group seeks to revive a case that they have twice sought to appeal.

The case has drawn national attention, with Riley Gaines appearing at a press conference Monday on behalf of the sisters and the Independent Women’s Law Center backing them as well.

The court did not indicate how or when it would decide the case. A key question during the arguments was whether the issue should be worked out within the organization internally, rather than in the courts.

The White House plan to give stay-at-home parents a childcare subsidy is still kicking up a lot of debate online. Advancing American Freedom , former Vice President Mike Pence ’s organization, is out with a one-pager urging conservatives to oppose the plan. More here .

articles.title: Kash Patel to tout 'largest' year-to-year violent crime drop in US history
articles.summary: FBI Director Kash Patel is set to tell senators the FBI delivered historic crime reductions, disrupted terrorist plots, captured top fugitives and overhauled the bureau under his leadership.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: FBI Director Kash Patel is set to tell lawmakers Tuesday that the FBI and its law enforcement partners have achieved what he calls the "most prolific run of crime reduction in United States history," according to his prepared opening remarks for the Senate Judiciary Committee's annual FBI oversight hearing. The individuals are among more than 4,260 arrests tied to Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs). Patel will also highlight that the FBI seized more than 3,258 kilograms of fentanyl, identified about 11,000 child victims and arrested more than 5,000 child predators and human traffickers. articles.title: Ossoff: ‘Compromised’ Trump won’t regulate AI
articles.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) on Monday said President Trump likely will not heed calls from technology leaders to implement guardrails on the development of AI because of his family’s investments in the industry. The Georgia Democrat pointed to venture capitalist firm 1789 Capital — where Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., is a partner —…
articles.body:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) on Monday said President Trump likely will not heed calls from technology leaders to implement guardrails on the development of AI because of his family’s investments in the industry.

The Georgia Democrat pointed to venture capitalist firm 1789 Capital — where Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., is a partner — and its investments in AI.

“They’ve invested heavily in AI labs. They’ve invested heavily in data centers,” Ossoff told MS NOW’s Lawrence O’Donnell. “So, the first family has a financial stake in this industry, and as a result, the president of the United States is compromised.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The president earlier Monday waived aside concerns raised by current and former employees of AI companies about the potential dangers of the emerging tech.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote Monday on Truth Social .

The criticism follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s announcement of a plan to slow the pace of AI development to allow for proper safeguards to be developed and implemented.

Trump, who is set to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week in Washington, cited U.S. competition with China on AI development in a separate post as justification to move forward with new technologies.

“President Xi, of China, just announced that China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future,” he wrote, calling the worries about the dangers of the technology “a HOAX.”

“AI, and Data Centers, will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History ­­— Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet,” the president continued. “It will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!”

AI is expected to play a part in the discussions between the two leaders at the upcoming bilateral summit.

Xi is reportedly bringing a large delegation of Chinese business leaders with him to the U.S., although it is unclear which industries will be represented by this group, according to Reuters .

When Trump visited Beijing for a bilateral summit in May, he brought a group of American business and technology executives, including then-Apple CEO Tim Cook and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.

Ossoff, who is running for reelection for his Senate seat in Georgia, called on voters to make their discontent with the president’s stance on AI known at the ballot box.

“We already know that Donald Trump is a dangerously corrupt and incompetent man,” the senator said. “The question is what we’re going to do about it.”

articles.title: Trump admin moves to gut Biden's signature environmental rules
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's EPA moves to repeal Biden-era carbon pollution standards, projecting up to $670 billion in savings for power plants.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's administration is moving to gut Biden-era climate regulations that it says could save the industry up to $670 billion in compliance costs. Environmental Protection Agency chief Lee Zeldin says the agency is repealing the majority of the Biden administration's greenhouse gas requirements for U.S. power plants. The EPA projects that alone will save $310 billion in compliance costs, and Zeldin has proposed eliminating all remaining greenhouse gas emission standards, which would save a projected additional $370 billion. The move, first reported by the Washington Free Beacon, is aimed at boosting coal and natural gas power production. The EPA says coal production for use in the power sector is expected to increase tenfold under the changes. TRUMP ADMIN AXES 'GREEN NEW SCAM' APPLIANCE RULES AS EUROPE BAKES IN BRUTAL HEAT "For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. articles.title: Democrats urge RFK Jr. to scrap proposed Head Start overhaul
articles.summary: Democrats are pressing Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to scrap a proposed overhaul of the Head Start program, warning the changes would weaken services for thousands of families nationwide. The proposed rule, dubbed “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs,” would “rescind and replace” the Head Start Program Performance Standards…
articles.body:
Democrats are pressing Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to scrap a proposed overhaul of the Head Start program, warning the changes would weaken services for thousands of families nationwide.

The proposed rule, dubbed “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs,” would “rescind and replace” the Head Start Program Performance Standards to “reduce regulatory burden,” “eliminate duplication with statutory requirements” and “reinforce state and local authority,” among other things, according to the Federal Register.

But in a letter to Kennedy, members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus argued that HHS’s proposed rule would “strip the Head Start Program Performance Standards (HSPPS) of more than 90 percent of its standards, likely taking away vital services from children and families.”

“It eliminates and substantially weakens federal requirements governing early learning, health, mental health, and dental services, safety standards, family engagement and family social services, and other services that have defined Head Start for six decades,” they wrote.

The lawmakers said the proposed rule would eliminate a federal requirement that children be supervised at all times, reduce mandatory annual training on preventing abuse and neglect and repeal prohibitions on corporal punishment, shaming, humiliation and seclusion.

It would also “require Head Start instruction to be conducted in English, with an exception for Tribal programs,” a move that lawmakers argue would weaken dual-language learning.

The letter had 70 signers as of Monday and is led by Democratic Women’s Caucus Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (N.M.), as well as Reps. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), Brittany Pettersen (D-Colo.), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.), and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.).

“Head Start ensures our most vulnerable kids have access to the care, nutrition, and health services they need in those early years. I am proud to be a voice for the parents, like me, who are enraged by the anti-family, backward agenda of this administration,” Pettersen said in a statement. “I will fight every effort by Trump to dismantle this program and work to protect Colorado families and kids across the country.”

McDonald Rivet said in a statement that “this Administration’s proposed overhaul will wreak havoc on what makes Head Start so special. It’ll make it harder for kids to learn, harder for teachers to do their jobs, and harder for working parents to make ends meet.”

The Hill reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.

articles.title: When a return to the office is a return to sex-discrimination
articles.summary: Return-to-office mandates do more than move bodies; they reshape exposure to bias.
articles.body:
The sound returns with the commute: elevator chatter, side comments in the hallway, the meeting where an idea lands only after someone else repeats it. During the pandemic, remote settings muted many of these slights. New evidence shows that wasn’t a coincidence.

A recent Organization Science study undertakes an analysis of everyday gender discrimination , finding that women experience far fewer gendered offenses when working remotely. As employers roll out return-to-office rules, the risk is clear: Mandates are not neutral. They can re-create the exact conditions that drive women out of roles, teams and entire fields.

Gender bias often hides in routine interactions. The Organization Science research found materially lower rates of everyday discrimination for women when remote, with the largest benefits for younger women and those working mostly with men. Their experiences improved sharply online, then worsened on-site, a pattern consistent with a less salient gender frame in virtual settings.

The core takeaway is not that remote work is perfect — it is that location changes exposure to bias. Why? Physical proximity amplifies unstructured interactions where interruptions, offhand remarks and assignment-drift occur.

A national poll on harassment found in-person employees more than twice as likely to experience sexual harassment as remote peers. When slights escalate, risk rises for companies as well. In fiscal 2024, the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission reported 88,531 new discrimination charges, up more than 9 percent year over year. That surge doesn’t prove causation from return-to-office mandates; it does underscore a compliance environment where re-exposing employees to higher-risk contexts is shortsighted.

Structured online workflows also narrow the aperture for bias. Virtual agendas, typed chat, and recorded decisions leave trails that make harder idea-stealing, selective credit and exclusion. Toronto’s Rotman School of Management describes remote work as a “protective shield” because it changes interaction patterns. Leaders who default to physical presence reintroduce unstructured spaces where bias thrives and documentation fades. For professionals charged with retention, engagement and legal stewardship, the office isn’t just a place. It’s a risk surface area.

Mandates rarely land evenly. In the U.S., high-profile employers are hardening stance: Amazon is enforcing an on-site regime per its widely reported five-day mandate , complete with badge-tracking scrutiny. Even when other firms retain hybrid norms, like Meta’s steady status quo , the gravitational pull of stricter policies is real.

These rules collide with unequal caregiving and commute burdens. The Federal Reserve’s 2024 well-being report links employment decisions to child care constraints ; mothers were more likely to report work impacts from care. Among adult caregivers, 67 percent struggle to balance jobs and care , according to one global analysis of U.S. workers. When you add uncompensated commute time and rigid arrival hours, the penalty compounds for women, who still carry disproportionate domestic labor .

Crucially, the preference data reinforces the equity case for flexibility. Women express stronger work-from-home preferences in post-pandemic surveys, including an IZA analysis of data from the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes. When mandates ignore that asymmetry, they don’t just raise attrition risk; they tilt opportunity away from a talent pool that has already asked clearly for flexibility. For leaders, that is both a recruiting problem and a brand problem.

The strongest case for a return to work in the office rests on development, mentoring and innovation. But here, the evidence points to nuance, not dogma. A National Bureau of Economic Research paper on proximity among software engineers shows real trade-offs: Proximity to coworkers increases long-run human capital development but reduces short-term output. The solution is not necessarily to shift fully on-site; it is to design for intentional proximity where it matters, while preserving flexibility that cuts bias and attrition.

First, protect flexibility as a default, not a perk. Research shows hybrid as a stable equilibrium, and women’s stronger preference for it is well documented. Second, import remote discipline into the office. Codify agendas, timeboxed turns and written briefs to curb interruptions and credit-theft. Third, measure exposure and outcomes. If harassment reports and bias incidents spike with more on-site days, treat location as a controllable variable and adjust.

Finally, be candid about the home front. Even as companies promise equal opportunity, women still perform more household labor. Policies that ignore this reality are not neutral — in fact, they redistribute friction toward women. Flexible scheduling, predictable team anchor days, and transparent assignment systems create access to the same developmental reps that proximity can offer, without forcing daily exposure to the most biased moments of office life. Leaders who tie promotion readiness to output, documented scope and peer-reviewed impact, rather than hallway-time, close the visibility gap that a return-to-office policy otherwise widens.

The evidence is consistent across sources: Remote and hybrid work reduce the day-to-day slights that wear women down, whereas rigid on-site rules reignite those frictions and stack penalties related to care, commute and safety. Development matters, but it does not require daily presence. It requires intent.

For the best results, firms should arrange to keep the bias-reducing benefits of remote work, paired with scheduled, purposeful proximity for coaching and creativity. And they should judge performance by outcomes. Do that, and you protect equity without sacrificing growth. Ignore it, and you will keep losing the very talent you claim you want to develop.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

articles.title: UT-Austin students fire back after Republican’s ‘blatantly racist’ post
articles.summary: University of Texas at Austin (UT-Austin) students fired back Monday against a “blatantly racist” post from the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, Bo French. French posted an image over the weekend of UT-Austin students, many of whom were South Asian, with the caption: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t…
articles.body:
University of Texas at Austin (UT-Austin) students fired back Monday against a “blatantly racist” post from the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, Bo French.

French posted an image over the weekend of UT-Austin students, many of whom were South Asian, with the caption: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

One student, Dhairya Gupta, who was shown in the images French shared, told The Dallas Morning News on Monday that he was “having some enjoyment” during the game but “now it’s just people being blatantly racist toward us.”

Gupta and his friend Rahul Kodali, who was also in the images French posted, said they were both U.S. citizens. Gupta immigrated to the U.S. when he was 5 years old and gained citizenship in childhood while Kodali was born in New York before his family moved to the Dallas area.

“Whether or not we are immigrants, that doesn’t change anything,” Kodali told the Dallas newspaper. “I’ve been an American my entire life.”

Gupta continued that he “thought it was surprising that people are going out of their way to be racist on that.”

“They have people voting for them, and they’re not scared to say this kind of thing,” Gupta told The Dallas Morning News. “It’s becoming to the point where this kind of racism just isn’t looked down upon as much as it used to be — or it feels like that.”

The incident has already been condemned by Texas GOP lawmakers — including Sen. John Cornyn and Rep. Dan Crenshaw.

“Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad,” Cornyn wrote on the social platform X .

Texas state Rep. Lacey Hull (R) urged French to delete the post.

“This post breaks my heart,” she wrote on X . “I see college kids cheering on their football team. I see Texans.”

Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R) urged French to delete the post and said the candidate can oppose immigration policies “without demeaning people because of their race or ethnicity –– this post has crossed the line.”

French, despite the broad criticism, has not apologized for the post.

He has instead used the backlash for campaign fundraising , saying on Monday, “The radical left and their allies are attacking me.”

articles.body:
FBI Director Kash Patel on Monday defended his personal travel and the law enforcement agency’s purchase of several luxury armored BMWs under his leadership amid scrutiny.

Patel is scheduled to appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday morning. Democrats on the panel are expected to press the Trump administration official over his use of government resources and the agency’s jet while in office.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), who chairs the committee, pressed Patel in May about reports that he used taxpayer dollars to fund his personal travel.

“As Director, I have reimbursed all personal travel and expenses and am fully compliant with and strictly follow the Office of Management and Budget rules,” the FBI chief wrote in a July letter, responding to Grassley’s letter, which was shared on social media Monday.

Several outlets reported earlier this year that Patel took a VIP snorkeling trip in Hawaii around the wreckage of the USS Arizona during a visit to Pearl Harbor last summer. Additionally, Democratic lawmakers pointed to other excursions the FBI director reportedly made on work trips, including a helicopter tour and jet skiing in Asia.

The bureau has pushed back on these allegations, saying reports of the helicopter trip and the jet skiing excursion were “both false.”

Patel cited former FBI directors’ travel histories and claimed that his decision to reroute agency travel through Joint Base Andrews and other government airfields had saved “thousands of dollars per trip.”

He also addressed concerns raised by Grassley and Democrats about the law enforcement agency’s decision to purchase several armored BMW SUVs over the FBI’s traditional armored Chevy Suburbans. Patel said the decision saved around $270,000 per vehicle.

Patel pushed back on scrutiny from Democratic senators on the Judiciary panel, accusing them of spreading “baseless political narratives.”

“Should they ever choose to participate in actual, good-faith oversight, then I’m committed to that as well,” he wrote. “Until they make that decision, I will continue to work with you as we have since my confirmation.”

“I have every confidence that we will continue to deliver fierce organizational accountability for the American people,” the FBI chief added.

articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees were told to pose as voters while searching for noncitizens on state voter rolls, according to a whistleblower report released Monday.

Employees were given sensitive information for people flagged as potential “unlawful voters” and instructed to search state voter bases, likely violating state law, according to the whistleblower.

The anonymous whistleblower report was released Monday by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (Calif.), the top Democrat on the Senate committee overseeing federal elections.

The senators received the 30-page disclosure last week, and they said it revealed “serious allegations of illegal and inappropriate activities” within DHS’s Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate.

It features information centering on a DHS effort called the “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” which uses federal employees to probe those suspected of illegally voting.

Some states restrict access to individual voter records. In Virginia, for example, users must certify that they are the voter or have the voter’s permission to access the information. The site warns that accessing another voter’s record is unlawful.

The whistleblower alleged employees were told to conduct the searches despite concerns that they could be violating state law, and they were assured individuals would not be held liable, possibly indicating that the agency was “aware that the activity may be illegal.”

Employees were also given less than two hours of training before beginning the work and were expected to review 40 people each day, giving them about 12 minutes per person.

The initiative was first reported by The New York Times earlier this month.

The disclosure warned that U.S. citizens and lawful residents could be wrongly flagged because of inaccurate or incomplete data.

Padilla and Schumer said the Trump administration is using the probe to interfere with upcoming elections and to prove President Trump’s long-held false claims of election interference.

“The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump’s long-debunked election conspiracy theories — and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it,” Schumer said in a statement to Axios.

“This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans,” he added. “Trump may try to steal this election, but we will make sure he can never be successful.”

articles.title: A Republican convention about fear collides with a midterm about prices
articles.summary: For all of the energy Republicans spent casting Democrats as radical communists, they left Dallas having answered a question most voters are not asking.
articles.body:
In a Reuters-Ipsos poll last week, 47 percent of voters said that the cost of living would be the single biggest factor in how they vote this November. Thus, when Republicans gathered in Dallas last week for their first-ever midterm convention, they had an important opportunity to show voters how the party would ease the affordability crisis.

Indeed, the Republicans had billed their convention as a showcase for its affordability agenda — no tax on tips or overtime, tax cuts and an economy they insist is finally turning the corner. However, the message that actually filled the American Airlines Center was not that Republicans would make life cheaper. It was that Democrats are too extreme to be trusted with power.

President Trump used his keynote speech to warn that a Democratic-controlled Congress would be a “communist caucus.” Majority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) took a similar tone — “These people are sick.” Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) described Democratic candidates as the most “dangerous, radical and frankly, weird” in American history.

So, lacking an appealing economic message, Republicans are betting that they can make November an election about fear of Democratic extremism.

To be sure, this strategy isn’t baseless. Fifty-six percent of Americans hold an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party, and 48 percent use the word “extreme” to describe it, according to CBS News . Democrats should take those concerns seriously, especially when the party appears more focused on ideological debates than the immediate economic pressures facing working- and middle-class families.

Where these tactics will fall short is that Republicans are in power at a time when poll after poll makes clear that voters’ overwhelming concern is the cost of living, not socialism. It also risks sounding disconnected from voters whose top concerns are not ideological labels, but grocery bills, rent, healthcare and gas prices.

To that end, even when affordability did come up at the convention, Republicans did themselves no favors. Trump continued his habits of mocking affordability concerns and asserting that prices are coming down. Yet the Consumer Price Index revealed that prices rose 3.4 percent year over year in July.

Likewise, Trump and other speakers put the blame for inflation on former President Joe Biden — despite Trump being in office for nearly two years, the impact of tariffs and the Iran war. As that war continues with no end in sight, pushing up gas prices and inflation, the failure of Republicans to communicate a coherent economic agenda or even show voters that they understand their pain will almost certainly hurt them at the ballot box.

With Republicans trailing key Senate races throughout the country, they know their best chance to retain control of Congress hinges on low-propensity voters who come out to support Trump but stay home when he isn’t on the ballot.

Desperate to turn out that base, Trump implored voters to consider the midterms as if he was on the ballot. That could mitigate some potential losses in deep red states and districts. But, combined with Trump’s offer of a $5,000 “dividend ” if Republicans win, also underscores Republican desperation and angst.

Not only are Democrats suddenly competitive in red states like Alaska and Texas, but Vice President Vance is being sent to Kansas to boost Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who faces a tough reelection fight in a state where Republicans haven’t lost a Senate seat in more than 90 years.

The irony is hard to miss. Despite two nights of branding Democrats as socialists, Trump dangled a government handout more sweeping than anything Democrats have proposed — one that economists predict would cost roughly $1.25 trillion, and fuel further inflation.

For his part, Vance came the closest to acknowledging voter discontent, though still couched in the convention’s unofficial theme of attacking Democrats. Speaking on the second night, he told the crowd , “Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

Coverage of Vance’s address emphasized that he appeared very much like the 2028 presidential nominee in waiting, but a landslide defeat in November will weaken his standing.

Interestingly, Republicans’ 2026 playbook appears to mirror what Democrats did during Trump’s rise: emphasize the threat posed by the other party while failing to offer a sufficiently clear and compelling economic alternative.

That did not work for Democrats in 2024, and it may be no more effective for Republicans in 2026. Ultimately, for all of the energy Republicans spent casting Democrats as radical communists, they left Dallas having answered a question most voters are not asking.

Americans may not support all parts of the Democratic agenda, but they are more worried about bills that keep climbing, gas prices reflecting a war with no end and a Federal Reserve on the cusp of raising borrowing costs to fight the very inflation Trump keeps insisting is receding.

Trump asked voters to pretend he is on the ballot in November, but on the top issue they say will decide their vote, he already is — and voters are not happy .

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die . ”

articles.title: Oil squeeze tightens as Iran-backed attacks cripple Hormuz escape routes
articles.summary: A drone attack damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline as Houthi rebels seize strategic islands near Bab el-Mandeb, squeezing oil routes beyond Hormuz.
articles.body: The U.S. is choking off Iran’s oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. But the routes meant to shield other Gulf producers from that disruption are now coming under pressure themselves. A drone attack last week badly damaged Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, a critical bypass that carries crude oil across the kingdom to the Red Sea. Repairs could leave it largely out of service for three to five weeks after it had been moving roughly 2.6 million to 4 million barrels per day in recent weeks. At the same time, Iran-backed Houthi rebels have seized additional territory and strategic islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean — adding pressure to another major shipping route already battered by years of attacks. And those repeated disruptions are already reaching American consumers. NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT U.S. diesel prices hit a record national average of $6.23 a gallon Monday, according to AAA, while regular gasoline averaged $4.32. Brent crude climbed as high as roughly $110 a barrel during the day. Washington has sharply curtailed Iran’s oil exports and trade, but the wider conflict is still disrupting energy supplies elsewhere in the region, especially as Iran-backed Houthi rebels strengthen their stance along the coastline in Yemen. THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE The question now is whether Iran is hurting enough to make the concessions Trump wants — and how much economic damage Tehran and its allies can still inflict while it holds out. The economic pressure on Tehran is mounting. Iran has gone weeks without sending meaningful new crude exports through Hormuz. Since the United States reinstated its naval blockade July 14, no Iranian crude cargoes have successfully crossed the strait to China, Tehran’s largest remaining oil customer, according to Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers.com. Iranian crude and condensate loadings fell to roughly 220,000 to 255,000 barrels per day in August, down from about 740,000 in July and roughly 2 million in March. Commercial shipping through Hormuz also remains deeply disrupted. Recent readings from Kpler, which tracks real-time data on global commodity flows and maritime shipping, have repeatedly put visible commodity-vessel transits in the single digits, even as the U.S. has worked to restore some movement through the waterway. Miad Maleki, a senior fellow with the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the pressure is increasingly reaching beyond Iran’s oil industry and into the broader economy. HORMUZ CRISIS HIDES A DEEPER OIL THREAT THAT COULD OUTLAST THE WAR "There are a series of indications" that the pressure is working, Maleki told Fox News Digital, citing the combined effect of sanctions, the naval blockade and growing diplomatic isolation. Iran depends heavily on trade through the United Arab Emirates and Turkey, Maleki said, and restrictions on those channels are making it harder to obtain foreign currency and essential imports. Gasoline could become an especially difficult pressure point. Iran remains one of the world’s major crude producers but lacks sufficient refining capacity to meet its own demand, leaving it dependent on imports that have become more difficult to secure. The regime can cushion some of the financial blow by continuing to print currency and pay salaries, Maleki said, allowing inflation to absorb part of the pressure rather than immediately cutting government payrolls. Physical shortages are harder to solve. But that does not necessarily mean Tehran has deliberately substituted the Bab el-Mandeb for Hormuz as a new source of leverage. Iran expert Arash Azizi said Tehran has already been forced to recognize that its ability to dominate the Strait of Hormuz is weaker than it once claimed. "Iran has realized that some of the leverage it has over the threat of Hormuz is gone," Azizi told Fox News Digital. "[Iran] is not able to close it effectively and is desperately trying to find a way to better its odds," he said. Azizi cautioned, however, against treating every Houthi move as part of a coordinated Iranian strategy to transfer pressure from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea. "Iran has limited control, and the Houthi-Saudi conflict has a dynamics of its own," he said. IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS Iran encourages and materially supports the Houthis, Azizi said, but does not exercise full operational control over the group. That distinction matters as the Houthis strengthen their position around Bab el-Mandeb. Their capture of Mayun Island, the port of Mokha and, most recently, the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands has expanded their reach around one of the world’s most important shipping corridors. Yet the group has continued to allow many vessels to pass rather than attempting a total closure of the strait. Azizi described the instability there as a "double-edged sword" for Tehran. Pressure on shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure can raise costs for Iran’s adversaries and increase anxiety in global oil markets. But a broader regional conflict can also make it harder for Tehran to achieve what Azizi described as its overriding objective: ending the war, preserving the Islamic Republic and beginning reconstruction. For Tehran, he said, the immediate goal is therefore less about opening a new front than improving the terms on which it can end the current one. Iran wants "some sort of a deal that puts an end to the war," preserves the Islamic Republic and allows it to begin postwar reconstruction, Azizi said. That shifts the central question back to Washington. The Trump administration has demonstrated that it can inflict severe economic pressure on Iran. What remains unclear is whether additional pressure produces the concessions Washington wants — and whether the costs Iran and its regional allies can still impose improve Tehran’s bargaining position or deepen its isolation. Azizi believes Tehran may already be prepared to move. "I think Iran is ready to make concessions," he said. "The question is, what concessions the United States would find acceptable?" He said Iran’s negotiating position has already softened from earlier in the conflict, when Tehran claimed sweeping authority over traffic through Hormuz. The regime’s principal red line now, he argued, is its own survival. Some Iranian officials may still believe continued pressure on energy markets and the U.S. economy could improve Tehran’s hand, particularly ahead of the midterm elections, Azizi said. But the imbalance in economic pain remains stark. "We are not hurting. Our daily life is not affected in a crazy manner by this war," he said of Americans. "Iran is hurting a lot more than the United States." "Iran is selling no oil," Azizi added. Azizi said the blockade, more than the administration’s latest sanctions package alone, has fundamentally worsened Iran’s outlook by restricting trade while leaving businesses with little idea when normal commercial activity might resume. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Maleki similarly said the regime can absorb inflation and financial losses for some time without immediately buckling. The more difficult test comes when financial pressure becomes physical scarcity. That makes the next phase of the U.S. campaign less about proving that Iran is hurting than determining whether Washington can turn that pain into an acceptable deal before Tehran or its regional allies find new ways to raise the cost of holding out. "They can keep printing rial," Maleki said. "But they can’t print gasoline."

articles.title: Why 90 percent of US baby formula lawsuits landed in two Illinois counties
articles.summary: IRather than a case built on sound science, plaintiffs’ lawyers built a business model whose cornerstone is a friendly courtroom that can deliver what the evidence does not.
articles.body:
Lawsuits against infant formula manufacturers have surged in recent years, alleging that specialized preterm formula causes necrotizing enterocolitis, a serious intestinal disease that strikes premature babies. This month, the first federal bellwether trial of the multi-district litigation reached a verdict : The jury heard the plaintiff’s evidence, weighed it and found that the prescription formula had not caused the infant’s untimely death.

Every one of these cases begins with a family that lost a child or nearly did, which is of course always devastating. But the most revealing pattern in this litigation has nothing to do with medicine. It has to do with geography: not with where these tragedies occurred, but with where the lawsuits are filed.

Roughly 90 percent of the nation’s baby formula claims have been filed in two Illinois counties: Madison and St. Clair. Both sit across the Mississippi River from St. Louis, with a combined population of just over 500,000.

Later this fall, the U.S. Supreme Court will consider whether to take up the question at the heart of that concentration: how state courts may reach in dragging out-of-state companies before its judges.

The cases piled into those two courthouses have almost no connection to them. The infants were not treated there. The families do not live there. In the case now before Supreme Court justices, the manufacturer moved its operations from Illinois to Indiana in 2018, but an Illinois court said it could still be sued there anyway, on any claim, by any plaintiff, indefinitely.

So why these two Illinois counties? Because the plaintiffs’ bar has done the math. Madison and St. Clair, along with Cook County, are ranked the seventh worst “ Judicial Hellholes ” in the nation by my organization’s foundation, the American Tort Reform Foundation. Their courts are known for lax standards on expert testimony, plaintiff-friendly rules for allocating fault, nearly limitless damages and juries with a history of returning multi-million-dollar nuclear verdicts. The same two counties already draw nearly half of the nation’s asbestos filings.

Trial lawyers know exactly where the hot spots are, and they file accordingly. The results bear them out. In federal court, where more than 800 baby formula cases are coordinated before a single judge under consistent and heightened evidentiary standards, the first case to reach a jury ended in a verdict for the defense.

In other Judicial Hellholes, juries have returned $495 million against Abbott in St. Louis and $70 million against the same company in Cook County this spring. The cases all involve the same science and same defendants, but they have wildly different outcomes. That is not a coincidence — rather, it is a strategy in pursuit of jackpot justice.

Illinois, unfortunately, shows no sign of correcting itself. The state’s highest court offers very little backstop and granted appeals in just 6 percent of cases in 2024. That is why this case has now gone to the U.S. Supreme Court’s docket instead. Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker also signed legislation last year opening his state’s courtrooms to even more lawsuits from across the country, further cementing its plaintiff-friendly reputation as a litigation hotspot.

This specialized formula for premature infants is typically only available in hospitals as prescribed by a provider. It is made by a handful of manufacturers, and every dollar drained into defending claims like these is a dollar not spent making it, improving it or keeping it on the shelf.

It is also safe. The American Academy of Pediatrics and other pediatric health experts continue to say that preterm infant formula is “indispensable,” “an essential, and often life-saving, instrument of neonatal care,” and that these lawsuits “ may jeopardize the availability of these formulas. “

Members of Congress also voiced concerns about supply issues in a bipartisan, bicameral letter late last year. American families who lived through the 2022 formula shortage do not need another supply shock layered onto an affordability crisis. Grieving families deserve better than to be treated as inventory and should not be exploited and preyed upon by trial lawyers searching for their next nuclear verdict.

Rather than a case built on sound science, plaintiffs’ lawyers built a business model whose cornerstone is a friendly courtroom that can deliver what the evidence does not.

It is now up to the Supreme Court to stop predatory trial attorneys from taking advantage of out-of-balance state judicial systems and provide the clarity and consistency needed to operate and keep a critical product available for families who need it. A lawsuit should be filed in the court with the greatest connection to the parties involved — not where a trial lawyer’s map says the verdicts run biggest.

Lauren Sheets Jarrell is vice president and counsel for civil justice policy at the American Tort Reform Association.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Monday that the Trump administration is “selling out” every American when discussing a Russian oligarch’s involvement in Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding. The lawmaker was asked what she made of Trump Jr.’s wedding in May being partially funded by Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who is linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin.…
articles.body:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) said Monday that the Trump administration is “selling out” every American when discussing a Russian oligarch’s involvement in Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding.

The lawmaker was asked what she made of Trump Jr.’s wedding in May being partially funded by Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who is linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“I mean, as we’ve seen, these guys are in the pocket of everyone but the American people. It’s profoundly disturbing,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “I said it two years ago, and I’m saying it again. This administration … they are selling out every single person in this country for a buck, and it’s disgusting.”

“And for what? To have a couple of extra frills at your wedding? It’s disgusting,” she added.

A ProPublica report published Monday alleged that Kremlev helped to pay for wedding expenses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, citing records and three sources with knowledge of the event. Kremlev reportedly helped rent an island and put up the money for a fireworks show at the wedding.

Model and influencer Bettina Trump, Trump Jr.’s wife, defended Kremlev’s involvement in the wedding, writing on social media , “Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.”

“It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” she continued.

The two married in West Palm Beach, Fla., according to Palm Beach County marriage records. The newlyweds then went to a private island in the Bahamas for a larger wedding celebration.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the ranking member on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has called for answers regarding Kremlev’s gifts.

“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas? Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers,” Garcia wrote on the social platform X .

articles.title: Vance: ‘Emily in Paris’ a ‘masterwork of American television’
articles.summary: “Emily in Paris” is receiving high praise from a seemingly unlikely fan — Vice President Vance says the romantic comedy series is “genius” and a “masterwork of American television.” The vice president lauded the Netflix show — which stars Lily Collins as an American who moves to the City of Light after college and navigates…
articles.body:
“Emily in Paris” is receiving high praise from a seemingly unlikely fan — Vice President Vance says the romantic comedy series is “genius” and a “masterwork of American television.”

The vice president lauded the Netflix show — which stars Lily Collins as an American who moves to the City of Light after college and navigates a burgeoning career and a roller-coaster love life — as a “massive cultural criticism of millennial decisionmaking.”

“If you’re just watching it superficially, ‘Emily in Paris’ is about this sort of bubbly girl who goes to Paris and has a cool job,” Vance said in a video posted on TikTok on Monday, describing his take as a “meta-analysis” of the series, which premiered in 2020.

Emily Cooper, the protagonist played by Collins, Vance said, “goes to Paris, and it’s obvious to everybody watching the show that she should end up with the French chef. She should marry this guy. They should start a family, whether in Paris or America. They should build a life together. That’s what they should be doing.”

“By the same token, the French chef should obviously end up with her, not the various craziest people that bump in and out of his life,” Vance said of the show’s culinary pro, Gabriel, played by French actor Lucas Bravo.

“And yet, what both of them do is they make a series of absurd, sometimes hilarious, sometimes not particularly believable mistakes, where she ends up with a bunch of random people or focused on her job. He ends up with a bunch of random people or focused on his job. And it’s like obvious: Fall in love, get married. You two were made for each other,” Vance exclaimed.

“The fact that they keep on making atrocious decisions is kind of like the best bit of cultural commentary — I would say cultural criticism of my generation, the millennials,” the 42-year-old vice president continued.

“It is — at the risk of overstating it — the Shakespeare of our time,” Vance said with a slight grin.

Netflix representatives didn’t respond to ITK’s request for comment about Vance’s praise of the show.

It’s not the first time that Vance has extolled the magnifique virtues of “Emily in Paris.” In a 2024 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Vance expressed his admiration for the series.

“I actually think ‘Emily in Paris’ is a masterpiece,” he said at the time.

articles.title: China expert warns Beijing wants Americans — not the CCP — to spread its message
articles.summary: A China expert testifying before Congress says Beijing uses American organizations as "Trojan horses" to make its influence appear homegrown.
articles.body: Congress will examine how foreign adversaries — particularly China — seek to influence American public opinion and policymaking at a hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. One of the expert witnesses told Fox News Digital ahead of the hearing that Beijing's greater advantage lies in shaping debate inside the United States through American organizations rather than direct Chinese propaganda. Matthew Johnson, a China expert and senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, said Beijing increasingly seeks to influence debates over national security and other strategic issues by working through American institutions and organizations, making its messages appear homegrown rather than directed by the Chinese government. HOUSE PANEL TO PROBE FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS "The idea is that it's not the Communist Party talking, it's actually institutions and individuals in the United States who are talking," Johnson told Fox News Digital. "That's actually the best outcome because then it looks organic... it looks like it's somehow being produced from within our society as opposed to by external actors." Johnson said one of Beijing's current priorities is slowing U.S. advances in artificial intelligence and data-center infrastructure—an area he said Chinese leaders view as central to strategic competition with the United States. He said China's influence strategy combines grassroots activism with efforts to shape thinking among academics, policy experts and other influential voices. His testimony comes as Congress continues examining the funding network linked to Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, whose nonprofits have become the subject of congressional investigations and a federal criminal probe. Fox News Digital previously reported that Singham directed at least $285 million into six pro-China, pro-communist nonprofit organizations beginning in 2017, including CodePink. Singham and the organizations have denied taking direction from the Chinese government, and neither Singham nor the organizations have been charged with wrongdoing. HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM Johnson is scheduled to testify Tuesday before the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, which will hold a hearing titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America." Lawmakers are expected to examine how foreign adversaries, including China, Cuba and Iran, may use nonprofits, activist networks and other organizations to shape U.S. public opinion and policy. "My goal is to raise the curtain to expose these operations and stop them from undermining our national security, capitalism and the American Dream," committee Chairman Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital. Johnson said the hearing focuses on what lawmakers describe as "malign foreign influence"—efforts by foreign governments to shape American public debate and policymaking by steering conversations toward their own strategic interests rather than those of the United States. "I try to break down influence in terms of looking at ways in which the framework of very sensitive strategic conversations is being steered in ways that seem to map onto China's strategic interests, not American strategic interests," Johnson said. He said the concept of a "Trojan horse" reflects Beijing's preference for influencing American debate through domestic institutions and individuals rather than direct government messaging. "From an American perspective, we want to be sure that it's Americans who are leading the debate on this issue, not Beijing," Johnson said. CHINA’S INFLUENCE MACHINE: FEDERAL RECORDS EXPOSE BEIJING’S PUSH TO SWAY AMERICA Among the organizations that have received funding from Singham's network is CodePink, the anti-war activist group co-founded by Medea Benjamin and Jodie Evans, Singham's wife. CodePink has spent years organizing disruptive protests inside Congress, campaigning against U.S. policy toward China, Cuba and Israel, and promoting its "China Is Not Our Enemy" campaign, which argues the United States should pursue cooperation with Beijing rather than confrontation. House Ways and Means Committee Republicans have accused the group of promoting narratives aligned with Chinese Communist Party interests, allegations CodePink denies. Asked why campaigns such as CodePink's "China Is Not Our Enemy" matter, Johnson said they promote an image of China that serves Beijing's strategic interests by downplaying the broader geopolitical competition between the two countries. "The idea that we don't want war with China, we want peace... these are all noble goals," Johnson said. "But... its strategic function is that it masks the fact that Beijing actually does seek a world order that is more shaped by Beijing in which the United States plays a lesser role." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Johnson said China does not have to convince Americans to support the Chinese Communist Party to advance its interests. Instead, he said, Beijing benefits when public debate shifts away from viewing China as a strategic competitor. "The real issue is whether there is actually a balance and whether we have enough transparency to allow us to assess whether there's a balance," Johnson said. Fox News' Asra Q. Nomani contributed to this report.

articles.title: O’Reilly predicts Paxton win: ‘Talarico is just too much’ for Texas
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday predicted that Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton will win his race against Democrat James Talarico, saying the latter “is just too much” for Texas. “So if I had to go by my gut, I’m not a betting man, but if I were, I would bet…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday predicted that Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton will win his race against Democrat James Talarico, saying the latter “is just too much” for Texas.

“So if I had to go by my gut, I’m not a betting man, but if I were, I would bet that Paxton will win in Texas because Talarico is just too much for that state,” O’Reilly told “On Balance” host Leland Vittert on NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. “He’s just too much. And Paxton is kind of smart just to hammer him and hammer him and hammer him because Paxton doesn’t really have much of a resume.”

O’Reilly remarked that Paxton became the GOP nominee in the race because Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) “wasn’t loyal enough” to President Trump to support his legislative priority, a GOP-led voter ID bill called the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act.

Paxton, according to the former Fox News host, “is a MAGA guy down the lane, and so he got the endorsement.”

“I don’t know anything that Paxton’s done to improve the lives of Texans, as you well put it, and he’s done a lot of things that are dubious,” O’Reilly continued. “So in a normal race, he’d lose by a lot, but it’s not normal.”

The Texas attorney general, who has a polarizing 23-year record in public office, has faced a series of scandals. The Texas state House voted to impeach Paxton in 2023, when he faced 20 articles accusing him of bribery, abuse of power, interference in federal investigations and retaliation against whistleblowers. A conviction on even one article would have ousted him from office.

But Texas state senators voted to acquit Paxton later that year, with two of the Legislature’s 19 Republican senators siding with Democrats to convict him on some of the counts.

Talarico is facing a favorable electoral environment as November’s general election draws near, with Democrats leading Republicans on generic congressional ballots, Trump’s approval rating sitting near record lows, and the unpopular war in Iran stretching past the six-month mark late last month.

The election handicapper Decision Desk HQ , a partner of The Hill, forecast Talarico has a 55 percent chance of winning the race as of Sunday, with Paxton holding a 45 percent chance of succeeding Cornyn.

The incumbent senator lost to Paxton in a runoff primary election in May, with Paxton having received Trump’s endorsement and marking the second instance in the election cycle that an incumbent Republican lost their primary without the endorsement, following Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.).

In endorsing Paxton, Trump said in May that Cornyn “was VERY disloyal to me … didn’t fight hard enough for the desperately needed SAVE AMERICA ACT.” The Texas senator also opposed the president’s call to eliminate the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act and dismissed the idea of adding it to a reconciliation package.

articles.title: NBC boosts security at ‘Today’ studio after string of incidents: Report
articles.summary: The new measures come after an intruder allegedly breached security in July and confronted a co-host outside the studio.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — NBC has increased security at the “ Today ” show’s Manhattan studio following several incidents, including an encounter involving a co-host and the unsolved abduction of co-host Savannah Guthrie’s mother from her Arizona home.

Page Six first reported the changes, citing unnamed insiders who said the safety updates were long overdue but have made staffers feel safer.

“It was much needed and took longer than people would have liked, but it does feel a lot better now,” one insider told the outlet.

Another source said “Today” staffers have been willing to follow the new protocols, despite the added security measures being more burdensome. NBC has not publicly detailed all of the new security measures.

The changes follow a July incident in which police arrested an intruder who allegedly accessed a secure area near the “Today” studio.

Later that month, Variety obtained an internal memo outlining some of the planned changes. NBC sources confirmed the memo was authentic.

One change limits guests to two accompanying people, including stylists, publicists, social media aides and other support personnel.

The July incident involved 41-year-old Andrew Truelove , who allegedly slipped past security and entered an area outside the “Today” studio. According to police, Truelove confronted Craig Melvin and asked where he could find Al Roker before allegedly directing a racial slur at Melvin.

Melvin alerted security, and Truelove was arrested. A security guard was reportedly fired following the incident.

Truelove faces charges including felony burglary and misdemeanor menacing in connection with the incident.

Court records show a man with the same name and age also has other pending cases in New York, including allegations involving an assault, trespassing and reckless endangerment on the city’s transit system as well as a 12-count criminal mischief indictment from last year.

The security changes come months after Guthrie’s mother, Nancy, was abducted from her home in Tucson, Ariz., on Feb. 1. She has not been found.

While the incidents are separate, the combination of the unsolved abduction and multiple security breaches has heightened concerns among “Today” staffers.

The latest changes at NBC’s 30 Rockefeller Center are intended to strengthen security for employees, guests and visitors to the studio.

articles.title: Trump wants a referendum on Trump ahead of the midterms — let’s give him one.
articles.summary: In Dallas, Donald Trump told voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” OK. Let’s do exactly that.
articles.body:
The strangest thing about last week’s Republican convention in Dallas wasn’t that Donald Trump managed to turn a midterm election into something resembling another presidential campaign. It was that so many people immediately began arguing about the spectacle.

Was this normal? Was it appropriate? Was it another example of a political party organizing itself around one man? What did it say about the Republican Party? What did it say about Trump?

At one point, Trump asked the audience to raise their right hands and pledge themselves to the “greatest president in the history of the United States” and to voting in November. Then, with his own hand raised, he declared: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like they do.”

It was weird. It was cringy. It was wildly inappropriate. And a sitting president joking about cheating in an election after years of making unsupported claims that his opponents do exactly that deserves criticism.

But it also illustrates something exhausting about American politics in the Trump era. Every provocation becomes the story. Every norm-breaking moment generates several days of outrage, defense and counter-outrage. Then another one arrives.

In Dallas, Trump actually offered Americans a much more useful way to judge him. He told voters to “ pretend that I’m on the ballot .”

Trump has spent most of his adult life asking to be judged as an executive. So let’s borrow an executive term and look, as impartially and dispassionately as possible, at his key performance indicators.

Trump’s approval rating now stands at 33 percent in the Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest level of his political career. He began his second term at 47 percent . Among independents, the numbers are particularly ugly. Heading into an election Trump has explicitly asked voters to make about him, independents currently prefer Democratic congressional candidates 36 percent to 22 percent.

Approval ratings are snapshots, of course; they are not history’s final verdict on a presidency. But they are certainly a KPI. So is the economy.

Trump returned to office in no small part because Americans were angry about affordability. Today, 71 percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living , including four in 10 Republicans.

Has the economy has collapsed? No. And there are areas of genuine strength for Trump; the border is unquestionably quieter than it was when he returned to office, and that is a KPI on which he deserves substantial credit.

That is what a dispassionate review requires. Count the wins. Count the losses. Do not move the goalposts for either. Then look overseas.

Trump ran as the president who would keep America out of prolonged wars . The United States is now in the seventh month of a war with Iran, w ith no immediate end in sight. The Strait of Hormuz has been severely disrupted. Energy prices have risen . The conflict has threatened to widen again through Yemen and another crucial shipping passage, at Bab el-Mandeb.

There may be legitimate arguments for confronting Iran. History may ultimately judge some of Trump’s decisions more favorably than voters do today. But that is not the KPI Trump originally offered. He promised something considerably simpler: strength would produce peace .

Trump spent years saying Russia’s invasion would never have happened had he been president. More importantly, he repeatedly claimed that his negotiating ability could end the war extraordinarily quickly. At times he talked about doing it within 24 hours , even before taking office.

He has now been president for nearly 20 months. The war continues.

American negotiators are still attempting to broker a settlement. Russia and Ukraine remain divided on fundamental issues . Ukrainians are preparing for another winter of Russian attacks.

There may be no American president capable of quickly resolving a conflict in which Vladimir Putin and Ukraine want fundamentally incompatible things. But that is precisely why the original promise matters. Trump did not campaign on the proposition that Ukraine was an extraordinarily difficult geopolitical problem requiring patience, compromise and years of diplomacy. He campaigned on the proposition that he could solve it, fast.

And that is the useful thing about applying KPIs to Trump. We do not even have to devise the metrics ourselves because, for years, Trump himself has supplied them.

Wars would end. Prices would fall. America would become more prosperous. Adversaries would respond to strength. His negotiating ability would succeed where traditional diplomacy had failed.

Some of those promises have produced results. Others plainly have not.

Trump wants Americans to pretend he is on the ballot in November. They should. Not because they adore him. Not because they despise him. And certainly not because of another week of arguments over whether his latest convention performance was normal.

Open the dashboard instead. Look at the promises. Look at the numbers. Look at the world Trump inherited and the world nearly two years of his presidency has produced. Then think about who should win in November’s elections.

Aron Solomon is chief strategy officer for AMPLIFY and has taught entrepreneurship at McGill University and the University of Pennsylvania.
