articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday slammed the Supreme Court ruling that blocked his mail-in voting plan, singling out the conservative justices who ruled with the majority.

Trump referred to the ruling, which upheld a judge’s block finding the plan unlawful, as “a bad decision” in a lengthy Truth Social post .

The president praised conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas as “legends,” noting their dissent against the ruling. However, he lashed out at “certain” other justices who “are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats,” apparently referring to Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett, who sided with the court’s liberal justices on the ruling.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal,” the president wrote.

Trump went on to predict the high court will go down as having “rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country’s history.”

While he voted with the majority, Kavanaugh suggested there’s at least a fair prospect that the plan is legal.

“But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections,” Kavanaugh wrote.

The decision marks the third time the Trump administration brought the plan to the high court’s emergency docket after groups blocked the effort.

The plan would have directed states to upload voter lists before sending out mail-in ballots. Additionally, the Postal Service would only deliver ballots that meet new design requirements.

“Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court, one that the Court System took forever to give, and then blamed it, in part, on no time left to implement a solution to our totally CORRUPT and out of control Mail-In voting ‘disaster,’ which is a laughing stock all over the World, and where we are the only country that has to endure such a Nation Destroying SCAM,” Trump wrote in his post.

articles.title: Trump approval ticks up from record low: Survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating has risen slightly after hitting a record low last month, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll released weeks before the midterm elections. Thirty-five percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance as the deeply unpopular Iran war reached its sixth month, up from 33 percent in a late August poll revealing…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating has risen slightly after hitting a record low last month, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll released weeks before the midterm elections.

Thirty-five percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance as the deeply unpopular Iran war reached its sixth month, up from 33 percent in a late August poll revealing his lowest rating across both of his terms.

The poll also revealed growing popularity for Democrats among Americans, as Democrats held a 7-point advantage over Republicans when U.S. voters were asked which party they would support if the elections were held today. Forty-four percent chose Democrats and 37 percent preferred Republicans.

The survey was conducted in the days after Republicans gathered in Dallas for the party’s midterm convention, where Trump sought to rally voters around keeping GOP control of the House and Senate.

Trump’s pledge that he made at the convention to provide Americans with $5,000 dividend checks if Republicans maintain control of Congress received little support in the poll, with 63 percent of Americans saying they disapproved of it — including 4 in 10 Republicans and 9 in 10 Democrats.

Trump has since defended the proposed payments, which could add more than $1 trillion to the national debt and would likely require approval from Congress.

The proposal fell flat with fiscal hawks in the GOP, who said they would not support handing out money to people who do not work or pay taxes.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey also showed a shift toward Democrats on the economy, an issue that has become central amid rising inflation and trade disruptions from the Iran war that have caused oil and gas prices to surge.

Thirty-eight percent of respondents said Democrats would do a better job handling the economy, compared with 37 percent who sided with Republicans. Reuters reported Democrats gained an advantage on the issue over the summer for the first time in about a decade.

articles.title: Newsom roasted online for 'staged' fly-fishing interview with CNN anchor where he dropped major 2028 hint
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's fly-fishing interview with Jake Tapper in Montana sparked social media mockery, with users calling the CNN outing staged.
articles.body: Social media users are taking jabs at California Gov. Gavin Newsom over his latest political stunt — a recorded fly-fishing outing with a CNN anchor that the Democrat used to break news about his often-rumored presidential ambitions. In the interview, recorded in Montana more than a month ago, CNN's Jake Tapper is seen with Newsom standing in shallow water, repeatedly casting fly reels while talking politics. Newsom told Tapper he wouldn't run for president if former failed 2024 presidential candidate former Vice President Kamala Harris tossed her hat into the ring. "Of course not. Why would I?" Newsom said when asked whether he would run against Harris in a presidential primary. "I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do it to me. Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to you." "I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time. Who needs that?" JENNIFER SIEBEL NEWSOM DODGES QUESTION ON HUSBAND GAVIN'S PRESIDENTIAL ASPIRATIONS Tapper pushed back, saying Newsom could do it if he really wanted to. But the Golden State governor replied by saying that would be a "gift from God for everybody else," likely referencing those who don't want to see a Democrat win in November, and claimed a primary against the former nominee would be "mutually assured destruction." "I know her base of supporters. I know her friends," Newsom said of the former U.S. senator from California. "The zen diagram (sic) on that is just pure crossover. It’s not — I wouldn’t do that to — I wouldn’t do that to people," he said, mixing up the Buddhist meditation practice with a Venn diagram, the visual tool where overlapping circles are used to show how groups are similar and different. KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY On social media, the reactions to the video widely shamed the pair for a stunt that was viewed as contrived. "why [sic] is newsom fly fishing in business casual?" an X user named Sam Alberti asked. "How lucky are we that a camera crew just happened to be standing in a Montana river while two guys who can’t cast pretended to fly fish," said a popular X user with more than 55,000 followers. "Totally organic. Not staged at all. CNN is doing the Lord’s work trying to make Newsom look like a regular dude. Herculean task.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​" Free Beacon reporter Chuck Ross wrote, "The best part of this is when Newsom says 'Zen diagram' when he was talking about a Venn diagram." "Jake Tapper and Gavin Newsom pretending to be regular guys fishing is absolutely hilarious," said another user with 1.7 million followers. 'HE'S SO THIRSTY': NEWSOM'S 'ENTHUSIASTIC' PRAISE FOR TRUMP POLICY TURNS HEADS "This is the most Gavin Newsom-ish fishing video ever -- the French Laundry of fishing!" said politico Kenneth Baer, referring to the upscale California restaurant where Newsom dined with a group of friends during COVID-19 lockdown despite his implementation on state-wide restrictions on social gatherings during the pandemic. "'Let’s do this interview surrounded by an entire film and sound crew in the river. Yeah, yeah, that’ll make us seem like nature guys,'" economist Nick Messenger said sarcastically. articles.title: Smithsonian move reignites 'woke,' 'Marxist' criticism as Latino museum avoids congressional approval
articles.summary: Mike Gonzalez's Heritage Foundation report alleges the National Museum of the American Latino promotes Marxist messaging and anti-Western ideology.
articles.body: The Smithsonian designated its Arts and Industries Building as the permanent home of the controversial National Museum of the American Latino, a move critics say will allow the institution to move forward without another congressional fight over a museum they argue should not exist. The decision comes as the Smithsonian faces intensifying scrutiny over its historical exhibits. Mike Gonzalez, a former Bush State Department official and longtime critic of the Latino museum, argued its inaugural exhibition promoted a far-left worldview and said selecting the Arts and Industries Building was an effort to avoid a contentious Capitol Hill battle. "We need to fire the Smithsonian leadership," Gonzalez said. "We need to get rid of the Latino museum. It needs to be de-authorized. It should not exist." WATCH: SMITHSONIAN DIRECTOR ADMITS SHE SEES HISTORY AS ‘TOOL’ OF ‘SOCIAL JUSTICE’ AFTER EXPLOSIVE HEARING Shortly after the interview, his wish partially came true when the Smithsonian's top official, Secretary Lonnie Bunch III, announced his retirement after four decades with the institution. Gonzalez examined the Latino museum’s inaugural 2022 exhibition, "¡Presente!," in a Heritage Foundation report shared with Fox News Digital. He also testified alongside National Museum of American History Director Anthea Hartig during congressional hearings in July. The Smithsonian declined comment on Gonzalez’s report or his comments to Fox News Digital. Gonzalez argues the location decision matters because the Smithsonian already controls A&I, unlike the National Park Service sites previously under consideration. "They want to use this as kind of a ruse," Gonzalez said, arguing that the institution can avoid another congressional fight by placing the museum on property it already controls. TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED Gonzalez examined "¡Presente!," and argued that a series of panels reflected what he described as an anti-Western, anti-American worldview. He pointed to its use of the idea "we didn't cross the border, the border crossed us" as historically inaccurate and said it is a favorite mantra of those on the left who criticize immigration law enforcement. He said the language casts U.S. westward expansion primarily through the lens of displacement while obscuring the history of Mexicans who remained in territory acquired by the United States and later became American citizens. "I guess your guest today would count as one of them," he said of himself. "Even though I don't… run around calling myself a Hispanic. I'm a proud American of Cuban heritage." SMITHSONIAN'S NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AMERICAN HISTORY PROMOTES 'EXTREME POLITICAL ACTIVISM,' WH REPORT ALLEGES READ THE FULL HERITAGE FOUNDATION REPORT His report also highlights exhibits dealing with gender identity, immigration and the veneration of Marxist luminaries and political figures. Speaking to Fox News Digital from Israel, he said such attacks on national identity would never "fly." One exhibit featured in Gonzalez’ report was titled "Jose Julio Sarria: Drag and Politics" and described Sarria as a "legendary drag performer [and] the first openly gay person to run for public office in the U.S." Another panel featured a Cuban transgender HIV/AIDS activist who fled the country during the Mariel Boatlift. SMITHSONIAN PUSHED ‘REVOLTING’ SOCIAL ACTION TRAINING AFTER ‘WHITENESS’ CHART APOLOGY: EXPERT "They create[d] a hothouse, an incubator of grievances among these 70 million Americans of Hispanic descent," he said, adding that Sarria and another featured figure prove that point. That example involves Orlando Letelier, a foreign minister under former Marxist Chilean President Salvador Allende. A photograph from the exhibition shows a 1976 quote from Letelier discussing his imprisonment under the Pinochet dictatorship and his later "liberation" in the name of restoring human rights. "Orlando Letelier has nothing to do with America, other than the fact that he died in a car explosion in Washington D.C., in 1976, but I'm old enough to remember that he was a cause-celebre of the left [then]," he said. "This is not an American story. The only reason he's there is because the curators who worked in this exhibit betrayed who they are... They're Marxists." Gonzalez, who said his father was imprisoned by Cuba’s former "tin-pot dictator" Fulgencio Batista before the leader was overthrown by Fidel Castro in 1959, said the Latino museum also does a rank disservice to the true history of Marxist-Leninist rule in Havana. "Havana perhaps has not been at war since the British invasion of 1763 and yet it looks like it’s been carpet-bombed: It’s been carpet-bombed by socialism." The exhibit on Batista omits the oppressive reign of the Castro brothers and also features a cartoon mocking the U.S. for the Reagan-era Iran-Contra affair, the report said. Gonzalez noted the latter aged poorly because the Daniel Ortega regime the U.S. opposed in Nicaragua is back in power decades later and has recently eliminated elections. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., a Smithsonian Regent and someone who also fled Cuban socialism, said the institution is a "crown jewel" of the United States and should be held to that standard. articles.title: Ohio city council joins the renaming trend with ‘Gulf of Cleveland’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has pushed to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” and Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”
articles.body: President Donald Trump has pushed to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” and Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” Now, get ready for the “Gulf of Cleveland.” Cleveland’s City Council voted to pass a resolution to rename part of Lake Erie as the “Gulf of Cleveland,” a satirical move poking fun at the president’s own renaming efforts. The resolution, spearheaded by council member Kris Harsh, does not have the force of law. A City Council spokesperson said the vote was 13-1. In Monday remarks at a City Council meeting, Harsh said Trump “is a man who clearly isn’t afraid to say what no one is thinking.” “I feel emboldened to take the extraordinary step of renaming Lake Erie as the Gulf of Cleveland today,” he said. The move is the latest instance of Trump’s critics pushing back on his unusual moves to rename bodies of water after the U.S. — or even after himself — this time through humor. While Trump can order the government to rename the bodies of water in official communications, he does not have the power to force international entities, or everyday Americans, to use the new names. “Keep in mind, there’s a very real person in Pennsylvania right now who wants to rename it the Lake of Pennsylvania,” Harsh deadpanned in Monday’s speech. “We cannot, as Ohioans, let the Pennsylvanians get a jump on us. It’s our lake.” Describing potential pushback, Harsh acknowledged Lake Erie is not a gulf. “And I say, ‘Who cares?’’ he said. “Listen to me very carefully and jot this down: Words don’t matter.” Harsh also joked that he wanted Apple and Google to “recognize our sovereignty” and depict the body of water as the “Gulf of Cleveland” on their maps — a jab at the companies’ decisions to change the names on their maps from the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” and from Lake Ontario to “Lake America” following Trump’s orders directing the executive branch to do the same. “Words don’t matter, but the whims of powerful white men like me do,” Harsh said, satirically. The White House did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment. In recent weeks, Trump has also shared a series of social media posts floating the idea of renaming New Mexico as “New America,” although he cannot unilaterally change the name of a state. The president’s decision to sign an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” came amid heightened tensions with Canada after the collapse of trade talks and imposition of tariffs between the two countries. The president’s executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico came on his inauguration day. The president also recently said he would declare the Strait of Hormuz a U.S. territory and floated renaming the waterway as the “Trump Strait.” Shipping through the strait, which borders Iran, has significantly dropped since the war with that country began, contributing to a spike in global oil prices. In another recent satirical jab at Trump’s renaming efforts, the creators of the comedy show “South Park” announced last week that they would rename the program to “South America” in the upcoming season. “Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA,” the show announced in a statement. In a Tuesday phone interview, Harsh told NBC News that “sometimes it seems like nationally the administration is equal parts cruel and absurd.” “As often as they do things that are just heartless and a gut punch to the American people, they turn around and do things that are just so ridiculously absurd you have to scratch your head and wonder if we’re living in a circus or not,” he said, pointing to Trump’s orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario. Harsh said he had also heard about a Republican effort to push for the federal government to rename Lake Erie as “Lake Pennsylvania,” appearing to refer to a resolution by Pennsylvania state Rep. David Maloney, a Republican. “I thought, if this is just going to race to the bottom, let’s just jump to the end of the line and see what’s the dumbest thing we can come up with,” Harsh said. “So I thought naming Lake Erie the ‘Gulf of Cleveland’ would be, just perhaps — perhaps pull back the curtain a little bit and let people see how absurd this entire thing has become.”

articles.title: Trump blasts Supreme Court 'disaster' after justices rule against him on mail-in voting
articles.summary: Trump called Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas "legends" for dissenting and listed Supreme Court rulings that have gone against him.
articles.body: President Donald Trump lashed out at the Supreme Court on Tuesday after justices ruled against his administration on a major mail-in voting initiative. "Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court, one that the Court System took forever to give, and then blamed it, in part, on no time left to implement a solution to our totally CORRUPT and out of control Mail-In voting 'disaster,' which is a laughing stock all over the World, and where we are the only country that has to endure such a Nation Destroying SCAM," Trump wrote. The president went on to praise Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, who dissented from Monday's order. Trump called the pair "legends." SUPREME COURT REJECTS TRUMP BID TO REVIVE STRICT MAIL-BALLOT RULES BEFORE MIDTERMS "It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left 'Dumocrats,' on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do – And now they have an open field to do so!" Trump wrote. Trump went on to list a series of cases where the Supreme Court has disappointed him, including its decision to strike down his tariff policies and void his executive order ending birthright citizenship. TRUMP CRITICIZES 2 SUPREME COURT JUSTICES BY NAME OVER TARIFF RULING "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court – it will likely cost me dearly for years to come – but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!" he wrote. The Monday order rejected the Trump administration's request for a stay in the implementation of a universal injunction against new mail-in ballot rules from the U.S. Postal Service. The rules would require federal ballot mail to be sent in envelopes bearing an election-mail logo, capable of being scanned by high-speed equipment and carrying a barcode unique to each voter. State and local election officials would also be required to submit envelope designs to the Postal Service for review and upload basic voter information to an online USPS portal. USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE Under the USPS rule, mailings that failed to comply would not be accepted and would instead be returned to election officials to correct and resubmit. The court's Monday order went unsigned, but Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a concurring opinion that allowed room for a potential Trump victory down the line. He nevertheless argued that it is too close to Election Day to realistically implement the rules for the 2026 midterm elections. "But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."

articles.title: Iran war has led to US munitions shortfalls, Pentagon inspector confirms
articles.summary: The inspector also found a bottleneck in resupply, despite President Donald Trump's claims that US supplies are "virtually limitless".
articles.body:
The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatly denied the US is facing shortages.

Trump has claimed US munitions supplies are "virtually unlimited" and said reporting otherwise is "fake news".

But the independent watchdog said the US spent more than $22 billion on munitions from February through June, leading to "strategic inventory shortfalls".

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment about the discrepancy.

The new report provides a first-of-its-kind, independent glimpse into US weapons stockpiles, data that is typically classified.

Over the course of the war, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks.

A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, found that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half.

The inspector general's report did not disclose exactly how many of the weapons remain.

It did, however, note the inventory shortfalls and reveal "industrial base bottlenecks" for munitions resupply.

The report added that the defence department is now working to "streamline procurement processes and production lead times" to address the shortages and "respond rapidly to a contingency".

Trump and other administration officials have sought to cast reports of shortages as false and "treasonous" .

In a 4 August X post, for example, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth described news reporting on the shortages as "not true".

And in a lengthy Truth Social post on 3 September, Trump claimed that the US had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition and is "stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen".

The watchdog's report also notes that equipment losses have totaled $3.7bn, with other $7.4bn in other expenditures. Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war from 28 Feb to 30 Jun.

Among the losses have been four F-15e fighter jets, a highly advanced F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed in "various circumstances".

When US and Israeli strikes began, Trump repeatedly said that the conflict would be over within weeks.

More recently, he said the conflict might not end until "right after" the November midterm elections in the US.

Polls show that the war is unpopular among Americans.

One Reuters/Ipsos poll released in early September found that only 23% of Americans - and only half of Republicans - believe the US to be in a stronger position with Iran compared with before hostilities broke out.

articles.title: ‘Still waiting on the DOGE check’: Battleground state voters cast doubt on Trump’s new $5K promise
articles.summary: Detroit, Michigan, residents call gas prices, car insurance and rent "ridiculous" while dismissing Trump's $5,000 dividend as political "bribery."
articles.body: Voters squeezed by rising costs are skeptical of President Donald Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend — with at least one resident pointing to a previous DOGE dividend proposal that never materialized. "I feel like that's a pitch to get more votes," Yolanda Lewis told Fox News Digital. "I'm still waiting on the DOGE check that he promised that we never received, so until he gives us a definite date saying when we're gonna get that and receive it, then I'll take that into consideration." Trump suggested in February 2025 that a portion of savings generated by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) could be returned to taxpayers, while Elon Musk entertained a proposal that envisioned payments of as much as $5,000. Trump later backed the idea of returning 20% of DOGE savings to Americans. DOGE reported $110.3 billion in savings from contracts, grants and leases, though a Government Accountability Office review later found that some of its estimates were inaccurate or lacked sufficient supporting evidence. Now, with affordability a top-of-mind issue for voters across the country, Trump has unveiled a new "Trump dividend" plan at the Midterm GOP Convention last Wednesday that would give $5,000 to American adults if Republicans maintain control of Congress. Several Detroit voters, interviewed by Fox News Digital at the Detroit Health Department’s annual Block Party on Sept. 12, rejected the proposal, with some calling it a "bribe" and others questioning whether the money would ever be paid out. TRUMP MAKES STUNNING FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND CASH PROMISE IN BID TO RALLY GOP VOTERS AT DALLAS MIDTERM CONVENTION "I think it's kind of irresponsible because what is the long-term impact of this money?" Jahdante Smith, the Green Party candidate for the state House of Representatives 9th district, told Fox News Digital. Smith, who supports Medicare for All, pointed to the nation's roughly $40 trillion debt in questioning how the proposal would be funded. "So where does that money come from? Where do you divert those funds from? Also, I think that it is sort of a bribe," Smith said. Michigan, which Trump won by 1.4% in 2024, has become a key battleground in the fight for Senate control as Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Saye and Republican Mike Rogers are both vying for Michigan's open Senate seat. El-Sayed called Trump's $5,000 proposal "unserious" during a rally in Lansing, Michigan. "Funny thing about it is like there's no world in which you can pay for it," El-Sayed said. "So how about you actually do some governing and like solve the Social Security problem. How about we guarantee people health care so they don't have to pay so much for that." Rogers' campaign did not directly comment on the former congressman's stance on Trump's $5,000 dividend plan. Instead, it pointed to El-Sayed's support for implementing a progressive tax plan. "You know what’s not serious? Challenging Mike to a 1:1 football scrimmage, taking money from Designated Terrorist Organizations and advocating to raise taxes for Michiganders while they’re already paying for Democrats’ mismanagement," said Alyssa Brouillet, communications director for the Rogers campaign. "Funny enough, those are things Abdul does." Prices are an acute concern in Detroit, where roughly a third of residents live below the federal poverty line. The city's median household income is below $40,000, according to U.S. census data. "Well, as a city Detroit retiree, affordability is very important, and I think the prices since Trump's been back in office have gone up on everything, especially gas, diesel, you know, affordabilities went out the window," William Davis told Fox News Digital. The current cost of gas in Detroit is $4.11 per gallon. Before the Iran war, gas prices hovered between $2.81 and $2.92 per gallon in January. TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME' Martesha Adams, a young mother and nurse living in Detroit, told Fox News Digital at the Detroit Health Department Block Party that she also viewed the $5,000 proposal as an attempt to win over struggling Americans. "The whole time I feel that he's been in the office, it's been a kind of game," Adams said. "America has been laughed at from everywhere. And the $5K for bribery, that's nothing. So I hope that people do not go for that bribe, and they really look into the politics." For Shelby Campbell, a 2023 graduate of Wayne State University, affordability has already forced significant changes. She said she sold her car because she could no longer afford Michigan's no-fault auto insurance and has struggled to find an affordable rental in Detroit. Campbell called Trump's $5,000 proposal "disgusting." "He shouldn't be able to offer people money if we have one party in office," Campbell said. "It's supposed to be about everybody and what we all want and need, so it's just bribery in my opinion." Campbell, who said she plans to vote for El-Sayed in the general election, argued that money already plays too large a role in politics. "I think he's genuinely a good guy, and he wants to get money out of politics, and I am all for that," Campbell said. "We seriously need that because big corporations buy our elections just like Donald Trump is trying to do." Other Detroit residents echoed Lewis' skepticism about whether Trump would actually deliver the proposed payments. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT Trump also proposed a separate $2,000 dividend last year funded by tariff revenue, though those payments never materialized. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I don't think it's realistic to think he's going to do that," Davis said of Trump's latest proposal. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Sunday on "Meet the Press" that the $5,000 payments would require congressional approval, while pledging to work toward Trump's proposal. "I never go out and give big commitments on the front end because I’ve got to work through it, and that’s what we do every single day," Johnson said. While Trump's proposal has garnered mixed reactions within the Republican Party, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, posted on X that he'd work to prepare a bill and get it passed before the election. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., rejected the idea that Trump was seeking to "bribe" voters. "The only thing that I knew of was that he has this concept of a dividend of all Americans being able to share in the success of America," Emmer told Politico. "Let the policy guys draft it. Let them debate it. Let them move it through committee," Emmer told Politico. "You get it to the whip’s office. We’ll pass it."

articles.title: Kamala Harris viciously mocked with resurfaced bumbling 'two words' explanation of AI after desperate call
articles.summary: Kamala Harris' rambling 2023 explanation of AI as "two letters" resurfaces after she posted a lengthy call to slow down AI development online.
articles.body: Former Vice President and failed presidential candidate Kamala Harris is being mocked over a resurfaced clip of her "two letters" explanation of artificial intelligence after she posted a call to slow its development. Harris, who previously served as the Biden administration's AI czar, posted a lengthy statement on AI on Monday. In her post, Harris called for President Donald Trump to "do his job to protect America’s interests by pursuing a treaty with countries like China to stop dangerous uses of AI, limit the speed of its development, and adopt global standards for testing." In response, social media users recalled Harris’ attempt at explaining AI as vice president in 2023. "I think the first part of this issue that should be articulated is AI is kind of a fancy thing," Harris said. "First of all, it's two letters. It means artificial intelligence, but ultimately what it is is it's about machine learning." WATCH: KAMALA HARRIS TORCHED OVER ‘ZERO SENSE’ WNBA PEP TALK IN LATEST ‘WORD SALAD’ MOMENT She continued, saying, "And so, the machine is taught — and part of the issue here is what information is going into the machine that will then determine — and we can predict then, if we think about what information is going in, what then will be produced in terms of decisions and opinions that may be made through that process." "So," she went on even further, "to reduce it down to its most simple point, this is part of the issue that we have here is thinking about what is going into a decision, and then whether that decision is actually legitimate and reflective of the needs and the life experiences of all the people." After Harris' X post on Monday, conservative influencer "Western Lensman" reposted the 2023 video of Harris, writing, "Kamala Harris on AI when it's not a written statement crafted by a team of consultants." National security and global economics expert Kyle Bass reacted, "There’s not a chance in hell Kamala wrote this. Have you ever heard her say ‘frontier,’ ‘advancing,’ and ‘intelligence’ in the same sentence? Until now, her misfits had never produced anything this un-Kamala and then posted it on social media." Columnist S.L. Kanthan wrote, "One of the dumbest women now wants America to voluntarily slow down progress in AI." He posted another video of Harris explaining cloud storage. Harris said, "No longer are you necessarily keeping those private files in some file cabinet that’s locked in the basement of the house. It’s on your laptop, and it's then, therefore, up here in this cloud, that exists above us, right?" Author and national security expert Sarah Adams commented on Harris’ AI post, writing, "No one is looking for your thoughts on 'intelligence.'" Another user, influencer Andrew Aziz, and several others suggested that Harris’ post itself was AI-generated. KAMALA HARRIS DIVES INTO MIDTERM FIGHT ONLY TO GET ROASTED FOR NEVER HAVING 'AN ORIGINAL THOUGHT IN HER LIFE’ In her post, Harris wrote that AI is "advancing at an alarming speed," emphasizing what she characterized as industry leaders’ call to "responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development." She wrote that "a slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest," saying, "Pacing AI development does not mean giving up on this technology’s potential to produce life-saving benefits in fields like medicine — some of which we are already seeing. Rather, it is about setting up sensible guardrails so that AI does not completely escape human control and endanger our safety and collective future." Besides action from Trump, Harris called on Congress to "work at an urgent pace" to provide AI oversight, saying, "The United States must continue to lead the world in developing AI technology even as we seek to impose common-sense safety standards." Harris is not the only prominent Democrat to have called for increased AI regulation recently. Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats during a private fundraiser in New York City on Thursday to place artificial intelligence near the center of their political agenda ahead of the midterms and the 2028 presidential race while warning that the technology could become dangerous without greater oversight as voters increasingly raise concerns about jobs, privacy and data centers. "This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous," Obama said. "If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future." ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN Meanwhile, Trump on Monday rejected growing calls for safeguards and restrictions on AI, declaring that the technology needs a "STRONG AND SMART" president rather than additional restraints. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so." Fox News Digital's Lindsay Kornick and Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

articles.title: Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz's 'effective altruism' network tied to AI regulation push
articles.summary: Billionaire Democratic megadonor Dustin Moskovitz-backed "effective altruism" funder Coefficient Giving eyes $1B artificial intelligence push amid doomerism concerns.
articles.body: Concerns about artificial intelligence spelling doom for the human race are being linked to a "cult-like" philanthropy movement known as "effective altruism" supported by billionaire Democratic megadonor and Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, according to a policy analyst. In response to former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation announcement on X, Parker Thayer, an investigative researcher at Capital Research Center in Washington D.C., went viral as he raised questions about whether the resignation was part of a broader network that aims to influence lawmakers and AI policy. "I resigned from Anthropic today," Coxon’s post read. "I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION Thayer quoted the post in a response that received interaction online with top lawmakers in Congress, including Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, D-Vt. "This post looks like the start of a VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion," Thayer posted. "The post is punchy, quotable, it almost seems professionally written. The first three accounts to quote tweet it all do so within 15 minutes of the initial posting." Thayer echoed claims made by White House AI advisor David Sacks that AI fears are overblown and potentially based on political motives. "I think this is becoming a panic," Sacks told CBS News correspondent Jo Ling Kent. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear. And I think this is a moment to really calm down a little bit and look at the issue rationally." SEN. BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE Coxon told Fox News’ Bret Baier last week that we are "on the doorstep of tremendous discoveries," but we're running in too quickly. He emphasized the need for moderation. Baier asked Coxon if the issue could be figured out. "I think definitely. I think if we actually try instead of submitting to the inevitability of a doomed race or a hubristic gamble, then we can solve it," he said. "The problem is not unsolvable." TOP MEDIA OUTLETS FAIL TO DISCLOSE WHO IS BANKROLLING THEIR AI REPORTERS Coxon said he was acting alone when deciding to voice his concerns about the direction of AI, according to The Wall Street Journal. Fox News Digital sat down with Thayer to ask about his theories concerning the coordination behind Coxon's "sophisticated" resignation, which was in turn met with a slew of national television interviews and immediate notoriety. Almost overnight, Coxon's post became a major point of policy debate spanning across political parties and politicians, including President Donald Trump and socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Thayer did not offer a theory for which individuals or groups might have coordinated with Coxon, who has denied such claims. But Thayer said the "AI doomerism movement" is associated with "effective altruism," a philosophy he described as "cult-like." OPINION: REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES According to the Centre for Effective Altruism, the movement is defined as a "project that aims to find the best ways to help others and put them into practice." But Thayer noted that while the philanthropic movement may sound high-minded, Silicon Valley elites and members who donate and support "effective altruism" may have much more direct political goals in mind. Thayer did not have evidence that any individuals or groups connected to the effective altruism movement provided public relations or other support for Coxon’s post about his resignation. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION Moskovitz and his wife Cari Tuna have been leading financial backers of organizations associated with the "effective altruism" movement. The couple founded Coefficient Giving, formerly known as Open Philanthropy, and remain its "main funders," according to the organization. Tuna serves as its president. Coefficient Giving says its artificial intelligence work has expanded rapidly, with $168 million committed to AI safety, security and field-building in 2024 and $351 million in 2025 — a combined $519 million. The organization says it is on track to commit more than $1 billion to AI policy advocacy in 2026. In a 2021 grant application description, the organization cited that it seeks "to fund programs and events in a variety of areas of interest to Coefficient Giving — including effective altruism, global catastrophic risks, biosecurity, AI for epistemics, forecasting, and other areas." Moskovitz, who Forbes estimates has a net worth of roughly $10 billion, contributed more than $50 million to support the Biden-Harris campaign from 2020 to 2024, including $46.89 million to the Future Forward PAC which served as the main fundraising vessel for the failed presidential campaign. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ On Monday, the Department of War Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering posted to X: "Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!" As for the reasoning behind "effective altruism’s" commitment to the artificial intelligence policy space, Thayer said the fear-mongering technique is comparable to the climate change narrative that has been traditionally peddled by the Democratic Party. "They basically just say kind of in the same vein as climate change activists like Al Gore used to, they kind of just make bombastic doomsday projections without citing really a whole lot of easily discernible evidence and just expect us to trust their expertise," Thayer explained. "First, they got you scared of the data centers based on a bunch of sketchy arguments about water pollution supposedly, and supposedly raising your electric prices, which don't seem to actually be true," he added. "And now they're getting you scared of the actual AI that the data centers are being used to launch." Thayer said that if AI critics were truly afraid of a potential doomsday scenario, they would be advocating for the extinction of artificial intelligence altogether. Instead, he says that it is a tactic to increase the government’s power over the industry while also acting in their own interest so "that they're the only ones who are allowed to build it." In an opinion piece published in Medium in 2024, Moskovitz noted that he was concerned about the potential risks AI poses, saying that a potential doomsday "situation may develop extremely quickly." "Contrary to the popular narrative about effective altruists working in AI, my interest in mitigating the potential risks isn’t rooted in specific predictions about the far future, but rather simple concern about the next few decades, when I and the people I care about are still alive to care about what happens," he wrote. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-LA, said a meeting at the White House to discuss AI policy could happen before the end of this week or the next. Trump also weighed in on the AI outlook in a post to Truth Social on Monday. "The people that say AI is going to destroy the World, and that Data Centers are bad for your neighborhood, are the same people that said, just a short time ago, that the World would be extinguished by "Climate Change." That HOAX never worked out for them, and now they’re on to the next one." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Moskovitz, Coefficient Giving and Coxon for comment.
